plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates the backpropagation computation graph for a neural network with four linear layers, laid out horizontally from left to right as a sequence of circles connected by arrows. The leftmost circle is labeled x_i (the input) and the rightmost is labeled ell_i (the scalar loss), with intermediate circles labeled with the upstream partial derivatives at each node: partial ell_i / partial f_0, partial ell_i / partial h_1, partial ell_i / partial f_1, partial ell_i / partial h_2, partial ell_i / partial f_2, partial ell_i / partial h_3, and partial ell_i / partial f_3, reflecting the chain-rule quantities accumulated during the backward pass. Each directed arrow between adjacent circles carries annotations below it for the local Jacobians needed to propagate gradients to the weights and biases of that layer, including partial f_k / partial omega_k and partial f_k / partial beta_k for k = 0 through 3; these branch off into separate annotations for the corresponding weight gradients partial ell_i / partial omega_k and partial ell_i / partial beta_k. All circles and arrows are rendered in black and white with thin strokes, giving the diagram a clean schematic appearance. This figure demonstrates the complete chain-rule decomposition used in backpropagation to compute gradients of the loss with respect to every weight and bias in a deep linear network.

interactionPlan.concept: The figure represents the backward derivative graph for backpropagation: each gradient node depends on downstream gradient nodes through chain-rule factors, while parameter gradients branch from the corresponding preactivation-gradient node.

interactions.label: Pass direction
interactions.teaches: The forward pass carries activations from input to loss, while the backward pass carries derivative information from the loss back to each layer's parameters

interactions.label: Animate backward pass
interactions.teaches: Gradients are not computed independently; each layer reuses the gradient arriving from the layer to its right and then branches it into that layer's weight and bias gradients
A selected gradient is the product of the downstream path back to the loss and the local derivatives encountered along that path

demo_steps.title: Forward computation sets up the graph
demo_steps.narration: In forward-pass mode, information flows from x_i through the hidden activations h_1, h_2, and h_3 until the scalar loss ℓ_i is produced. These forward quantities are the values whose local derivatives will be reused during backpropagation.

demo_steps.title: Backward pass starts at the loss
demo_steps.narration: Switch to backward-pass mode: the direction reverses, and the loss seeds the chain of gradients. The first highlighted terms show how ∂ℓ_i/∂f_3 and ∂ℓ_i/∂h_3 are obtained before moving to earlier layers.

demo_steps.title: Each layer branches into parameter gradients
demo_steps.narration: As the backward signal reaches each ∂ℓ_i/∂f_k node, it splits downward to form ∂ℓ_i/∂β_k and ∂ℓ_i/∂ω_k by multiplying by the local derivatives ∂f_k/∂β_k and ∂f_k/∂ω_k.

demo_steps.title: Click a gradient to see its dependency chain
demo_steps.narration: Clicking a node such as ∂ℓ_i/∂h_2 highlights the exact path of derivatives that must be multiplied to obtain it, making the chain rule visible as a route through the graph.

plan.keyInsight: Backpropagation is dynamic programming for the chain rule: once a downstream gradient is known, the same quantity is reused to compute both the next upstream gradient and that layer's parameter gradients.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a wide horizontal black-and-white schematic with thin black circular nodes and left-pointing arrows for the backward chain. Place x_i alone at the far left and ℓ_i at the far right; arrange the derivative nodes between them in the order ∂ℓ_i/∂f_0, ∂ℓ_i/∂h_1, ∂ℓ_i/∂f_1, ∂ℓ_i/∂h_2, ∂ℓ_i/∂f_2, ∂ℓ_i/∂h_3, ∂ℓ_i/∂f_3. Under each ∂ℓ_i/∂f_k node, draw two smaller lower circles for ∂ℓ_i/∂β_k and ∂ℓ_i/∂ω_k with diagonal downward arrows labeled by the corresponding local derivatives ∂f_k/∂β_k and ∂f_k/∂ω_k. Keep the base diagram monochrome, then use a single accent color such as blue for forward-pass highlights and orange for backward-pass highlights; clicking should brighten the selected node and trace its dependency path back to ℓ_i plus any relevant local derivative labels.
